summary.text: Lesson 7 of Wordly Wise 3000 Book 9: fifteen words about criticism and disapproval (belittle, censure, expostulate, ingrate), excess and luxury (exorbitant, sumptuous, voluble), decline and consequence (moribund, fateful), plus amorous, deem, divulge, injunction, motif and subsidize.

why.text: This lesson is full of near-miss traps — censure/censor, fateful/fatal — the exact pairs standardized tests build questions around. Getting them straight once is worth more than a dozen easier words.

objectives.text: Define and use all fifteen Lesson 7 words correctly
Distinguish censure from censor and fateful from fatal
Choose between an everyday and a technical sense of the same word
Apply the “lacks” analogy relationship to people as well as things

parentNote.text: Built from the Lesson 7 word list. Two near-miss pairs are the real content here: censure (criticize) versus censor (suppress), and fateful (momentous) versus fatal (deadly). Both get their own question because both are standard test traps. The SUMPTUOUS : SPARTAN analogy reaches back to Lesson 4 on purpose — vocabulary that only works inside its own lesson has not really been learned.

nextUp.text: Cards, then the quiz. Write censure and censor side by side once — that pair costs people marks.

cards.def:
**Expressing love or the state of being in love.** (adjective)
• The couple exchanged amorous glances across the dinner table.
• Amor is Latin for love — the same root under amiable and enamoured.

**To present or speak of as unimportant or of little value.** (verb)
• "Why do you make your efforts seem bigger by belittling mine?" she complained.
• Literally to make little — the word says exactly what it does.

**To blame or find fault with.** (verb)
• The judge censured the lawyer for failing to file the papers on time.
• As a noun: severe criticism — divorce once carried far greater censure than it does today.
cards.hint: Censure is criticism; censor is suppression. One word apart, two different acts.

cards.def:
**To consider; to believe.** (verb)
• The mayor deemed it prudent to call up emergency crews from neighbouring counties.
• Deeming is judging — it always reports someone’s conclusion.

**To make known something secret; to reveal.** (verb)
• Blackbeard divulged the location of the buried treasure to no one.
• The secrecy is required — you cannot divulge something already public.

**Exceeding normal bounds; more than seems reasonable.** (adjective)
• Two hundred dollars seems an exorbitant price for a shirt.
• Ex- plus orbit: it has gone outside the normal orbit.

**To argue earnestly in an attempt to dissuade or show strong disapproval.** (verb)
• My friends expostulated with me about waiting until the storm passed before walking to the park.
• You expostulate WITH a person, trying to talk them out of something.

**Having great or significant consequences.** (adjective)
• The article examines Truman’s fateful decision to drop the atomic bomb.
• Not the same as fatal — a fateful choice is momentous, not necessarily deadly.

**An ungrateful person.** (noun)
• I felt like an ingrate for forgetting to thank my mother for making the food for my party.
• Grat- is the root of gratitude and grateful; in- cancels it.

**An order or command.** (noun)
• My family heeded the injunction to evacuate the island.
• Second meaning: a court order prohibiting someone from doing something.

**Close to death; in a dying state.** (adjective)
• The company was moribund when it was taken over last year.
• Mor- is death, as in mortal — used for institutions and ideas as often as for bodies.

**A theme or idea developed or repeated in a work of art or literature.** (noun)
• Throughout the novel, the author explores the motif of separation.
• Second meaning: a repeated design — the nursery wallpaper had a rabbit motif.
cards.hint: A motif RECURS. One mention is not a motif.

cards.def:
**To support by giving financial aid.** (verb)
• Crowdfunding has subsidized countless arts projects.
• subsidy (n): a grant of money, often from a government, to a group or individual.

**Extravagantly splendid or costly; luxurious.** (adjective)
• After the wedding we enjoyed a sumptuous meal in the hotel dining room.
• The exact opposite of Spartan, from Lesson 4.

**Characterized by a ready flow of words; talkative.** (adjective)
• The voluble host scarcely gave his guests a chance to speak.
• It describes the flow of speech, not its quality.

questions.q: To belittle someone’s work is to:
questions.hint: The word says what it does.
steps: Belittle means to present or speak of something as unimportant or of little value.
Making your own efforts look bigger by belittling someone else's is the book's example.
Praising highly is extol, from Lesson 1 — the exact opposite.

ex.main: **Speak of it as unimportant.** Belittle literally means to make little of something.
ex.tip: Belittle and extol are a matched pair across two lessons. Linking them costs nothing and buys both.

questions.q: An exorbitant price is one that is:
steps: Exorbitant means exceeding normal bounds; more than seems reasonable.
Two hundred dollars for a shirt is the book's example of a price outside the normal range.
The word is a judgement about excess, not about how the price is set or paid.

ex.main: **Far beyond what seems reasonable.** It has left the normal orbit — that is the image inside the word.
ex.tip: Exorbitant always carries disapproval. Nobody calls their own prices exorbitant.

questions.q: An ingrate is a person who is:
questions.hint: The root is the same as in gratitude.
steps: An ingrate is an ungrateful person.
Feeling like an ingrate for forgetting to thank your mother is the book's example.
The prefix in- cancels the grat- root that gives us grateful and gratitude.

ex.main: **Ungrateful.** Grat- means thanks; in- negates it.
ex.tip: Negating prefixes (in-, un-, dis-, a-) are worth spotting instantly. They flip a root you already know.

questions.q: A moribund industry is one that is:
steps: Moribund means close to death; in a dying state.
A company described as moribund before a takeover was barely surviving.
The root mor- is the same one in mortal and mortality.

ex.main: **Close to dying out.** Moribund applies to institutions and ideas as readily as to living things.
ex.tip: Mor- (death) shows up in mortal, mortuary, moribund and mortify. One root, four words.

questions.hint: The information must have been secret first.
steps: Divulge means to make known something secret; to reveal.
Blackbeard divulging the treasure's location to no one means he revealed it to nobody.
The secrecy is a requirement — you cannot divulge public knowledge.

ex.main: **Reveal something that was secret.** If it was never secret, divulge is the wrong verb.
ex.tip: Some verbs carry preconditions. Divulge requires prior secrecy the way recuperate requires prior illness.

questions.q: A voluble speaker is one who:
questions.hint: It describes the flow, not the quality.
steps: Voluble means characterized by a ready flow of words; talkative.
A voluble host scarcely letting guests speak is the book's example.
The word says nothing about whether the talk is good — only that there is a lot of it.

ex.main: **Talks readily and at length.** Voluble measures flow, not worth.
ex.tip: Notice which words judge quality and which only measure quantity. Voluble is quantity.

questions.q: A judge "censured" an attorney. This means the judge:
opts: Removed the attorney from the case
questions.hint: Careful — censure and censor are different words.
steps: Censure means to blame or find fault with.
A judge censuring a lawyer for filing late is delivering formal criticism.
Suppressing material is CENSOR — a different word one letter away.
Censure is a rebuke, not a removal or a suppression.

ex.main: **Formally criticized the attorney.** Censure is criticism; censor is suppression. The pair is a favourite test trap.
ex.tip: Near-identical words with different meanings are worth writing side by side once: censure/censor, adapt/adopt, elicit/illicit.

questions.q: A historian calls a decision "fateful." She means it was:
opts: Made by chance rather than reason
questions.hint: Fateful and fatal are not the same word.
steps: Fateful means having great or significant consequences.
Truman's fateful decision was momentous — it shaped what followed.
Fatal means causing death; fateful means carrying great weight. A fateful decision can save lives.

ex.main: **Momentous, with far-reaching consequences.** Fateful is about magnitude of consequence, not about death.
ex.tip: Fateful/fatal is the same trap family as censure/censor. Sharing a root does not mean sharing a meaning.

questions.q: Which sentence uses injunction in its LEGAL sense?
opts: The court issued an injunction barring the company from cutting the trees
She heeded her grandmother’s injunction to write thank-you notes
The sign carried an injunction against feeding the ducks
His injunction to be careful went unheeded
questions.hint: One sense is any command; the other is specifically a court order.
steps: An injunction is an order or command; in law it is specifically a court order prohibiting something.
A court barring a company from cutting trees is precisely that legal sense.
Grandmothers, signs and friends can all issue commands, but none of those is a court order.

ex.main: **The court order barring tree-cutting.** The legal sense needs a court behind it.
ex.tip: A word can have an everyday sense and a technical one. When a question names the field, use that field's sense.

questions.hint: These two verbs pull in opposite directions.
steps: To belittle is to make something seem unimportant; to praise is to raise it up. Opposites.
So the pattern is: antonyms.
To censure is to find fault; to commend is to speak approvingly. Opposites. Match.
Sumptuous means luxurious, divulge means reveal, and an ingrate IS ungrateful — all three are synonym pairs.

ex.main: **Both pairs are ANTONYMS.** Belittle and praise reverse each other, as do censure and commend.
ex.tip: When three options are synonyms and one is an antonym, work out the stem first — it usually points at the odd one.

questions.hint: Lesson 4 gave you one of these words. Are they alike or opposite?
steps: Sumptuous means extravagantly luxurious; Spartan (Lesson 4) means plain and without luxury. Opposites.
So the relationship is antonyms.
Exorbitant means far more than reasonable; cheap means far less. Opposites. Match.
Voluble means talkative, moribund means dying, and a motif is a theme — three synonym pairs.

ex.main: **Both pairs are ANTONYMS on the same scale.** Sumptuous and Spartan measure luxury; exorbitant and cheap measure cost.
ex.tip: The strongest antonym pairs sit at opposite ends of ONE scale. Naming the scale confirms the pair.

questions.hint: What does an ingrate not have?
steps: An ingrate is a person defined by LACKING gratitude.
So the pattern is: person : the quality they lack.
A miser is a person defined by lacking generosity. Match.
An orator delivers a speech, a proponent gives support, and a motif involves repetition — all three POSSESS or produce, rather than lack.

ex.main: **Both pairs are PERSON : THE QUALITY THEY LACK.** An ingrate has no gratitude; a miser has no generosity.
ex.tip: This is the “lacks” relationship again, now applied to people. The same handful of relationships covers most analogies you will meet.

questions.q: A friend "expostulated with" you about a plan. What did the friend do?
opts: Argued earnestly to talk you out of it
Reported it to someone in authority
Explained it to you for the first time
questions.hint: The phrase "with you" is doing work here.
steps: Expostulate means to argue earnestly in an attempt to dissuade or show strong disapproval.
You expostulate WITH a person — the preposition marks the person being talked to.
The goal is dissuasion, so the friend was trying to change your mind, not agree or report.

ex.main: **Argued earnestly to talk you out of it.** Expostulating is disapproval delivered face to face, aimed at changing a decision.
ex.tip: Prepositions carry meaning: expostulate WITH a person ABOUT a plan. Learning the pattern prevents misuse.

questions.q: In a novel, "the motif of separation" appears in chapters 2, 9, and 21. Why is motif the right word rather than "event"?
opts: A motif is an idea that recurs across a work, not a single occurrence
A motif must always be visual rather than thematic
A motif is only used for poetry, never novels
A motif means the same thing as the plot
questions.hint: What does appearing three times establish?
steps: A motif is a theme or idea that is developed or REPEATED in a work.
Appearing in three separate chapters is exactly that recurrence.
A single event in chapter 2 would just be an event; the return in 9 and 21 is what makes it a motif.
Motifs can be visual or thematic, and appear in every form of art.

ex.main: **A motif recurs; an event happens once.** The repetition is what earns the word.
ex.tip: Literary terms are precise. If a question asks why one term fits better, the answer is usually in the definition's fine print.

questions.hint: How far apart are these two in meaning?
steps: Moribund means close to death, in a dying state — the two words mean nearly the same thing.
So the relationship is synonyms.
Voluble means characterized by a ready flow of words: talkative. Same meaning. Match.
Belittle and praise are opposites, an ingrate lacks gratitude, and censure delivers criticism.

ex.main: **Both pairs are SYNONYMS.** Moribund and dying overlap almost completely, as do voluble and talkative.
ex.tip: Three different relationships sit in the wrong options here. Naming the stem first is what stops you being pulled toward whichever pair simply feels related.

questions.q: To deem something prudent is to:
opts: Consider or judge it to be prudent
steps: Deem means to consider; to believe.
The mayor deeming it prudent to call up emergency crews reports her judgement, not a proof.
Deeming is always someone's conclusion, which is why it needs a person behind it.

ex.main: **Consider or judge it to be prudent.** Deem reports what someone concluded, not what was demonstrated.
ex.tip: Watch for verbs that attribute a judgement. They tell you a claim is someone's view, not established fact.

questions.q: To subsidize a project is to:
opts: Cancel it for lack of funds
questions.hint: A subsidy is a grant of money.
steps: Subsidize means to support by giving financial aid.
Crowdfunding subsidizing arts projects means money flowing in to keep them going.
subsidy (n) is the grant itself, often given by a government.

ex.main: **Support it with financial aid.** Subsidizing keeps something running that might not survive on its own.
ex.tip: Subsidize describes the direction of money. Nothing in the word says whether the support is deserved.

opts: The letters between them grew steadily more amorous over the summer
She gave the machine an amorous kick when it jammed
The amorous storm lasted three days
He made an amorous calculation of the total cost
steps: Amorous means expressing love or being in love.
Letters growing more amorous over a summer is the word in its natural setting.
Kicks, storms and calculations cannot express love.

ex.main: **The letters grew more amorous.** Amorous attaches to expressions of love — glances, letters, tones.
ex.tip: The root amor also gives amiable, enamoured and amateur (originally, one who does it for love).

questions.q: A newspaper writes that a proposal met "vociferous censure from a voluble opponent." Unpack what that says.
opts: Loud criticism from someone who talks a great deal
Quiet criticism from someone who rarely speaks
Loud praise from someone who talks a great deal
Legal suppression by someone in authority
questions.hint: Three Lesson 6 and 7 words are stacked here. Take them one at a time.
steps: Vociferous (Lesson 6) means making feelings known loudly.
Censure means to blame or find fault — criticism, not praise.
Voluble means characterized by a ready flow of words: talkative.
Stacked together: loud criticism from a talkative opponent. Note it is censure, not censor — criticism, not suppression.

ex.main: **Loud criticism from a talkative opponent.** The censure/censor distinction is what rules out the suppression option.
ex.tip: Dense sentences are easier taken one word at a time. Translate each, then reassemble.
